title: Something before heaven
hookLine: something formed before heaven and earth; the Tao follows what is so of itself (Tao Te Ching 25)

lines: IT JUST DID WHAT IT DOES.
cards: A plant on a kitchen windowsill. Nobody turned it. Nobody gave it instructions.
But over a few weeks every leaf has swung around to face the glass, the stems leaning toward the light like people at a parade barrier. It didn't try. It didn't decide.
It just did what a plant does. Chapter twenty-five of the Tao Te Ching reaches back before the world began, and then lands on something as ordinary as that plant: a thing being what it is.

teach.b: First, something before heaven. In Legge's translation the chapter opens: "There was something undefined and complete, coming into existence before Heaven and Earth."
Still, formless, standing alone, it says, not changing, going everywhere without wearing out. It could be called the mother of everything under heaven.

teach.h: NO NAME, SO CALL IT THE WAY.
teach.b: Second, no name, so call it the Way. Then the speaker admits a problem. He doesn't know its name.
So he calls it Tao, the Way, and if pushed for a name, he calls it great. And great, the chapter says, means it goes far out, and going far out, it comes back.

teach.h: EACH TAKES ITS LAW FROM THE NEXT.
teach.b: Third, each takes its law from the next. Near the end comes a chain. People follow the earth.
The earth follows heaven. Heaven follows the Way. You'd expect the chain to stop there, at the top.
The last link, in Legge's words: "The law of the Tao is its being what it is." The Chinese word there is ziran. Translators render it as what is so of itself, or naturalness, or spontaneity.
Not a higher power above the Way, but the Way simply being itself, the way the plant leans toward the window without being told.

So the chapter climbs past heaven, and at the very top finds no ruler at all, only something doing what it does. Some readers take this as a key to the whole book: the deepest thing isn't forced, and doesn't force.

how: In Taoist thought, ziran, being so of itself, is an ideal: some practitioners spend time in nature or in quiet watching to sense how things unfold without being forced.

o: what is so of itself: things being what they are
a hidden force that pushes all things to change
a strict law that heaven lays down for the world

s: chapter twenty-five gives the Way its true, secret name
the speaker says he doesn't know its name, so he calls it the Way, and if pushed, great.
in the chapter, the chain ends with the Way following what is so of itself
"the law of the Tao is its being what it is," in Legge's words.
the chapter says the thing before heaven was noisy and always changing
it calls it still, formless, standing alone, not changing.

games.q: people follow the earth. the earth follows heaven. heaven follows the Way. what does the Way follow?
o: ziran: what is so of itself.
games.why: the chain goes past heaven and finds no ruler at the top, only the Way being what it is.

practice: Find something alive nearby, a plant, a tree out the window, your own breath, and just watch it, without helping or judging. Notice how much is happening with no effort from you at all.
If your mind starts to manage, let it rest and go back to watching.

wordCard.voice: Ziran. What is so of itself: naturalness, the way a thing is when nothing is pushing it. In chapter twenty-five, it's what even the Way follows. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, zìrán: so of itself, naturalness. In Tao Te Ching 25 the Way follows it.

carryVoice: Your line: so of itself. At the top of the chain, nothing is pushing. Go gently.
